title: Logic gates from a single NAND
task: Using only `nand(a, b)` (given) and your own gates, write `not_(a)`, `and_(a, b)`, `or_(a, b)` and `xor_(a, b)`. Each takes bits (0 or 1) and returns a bit. No Python operators, `if`, or comparisons: just calls.
hints: `and_` is the opposite of `nand`, and you just built "opposite": `not_(nand(a, b))`.
For `or_`, use De Morgan: a or b = not (not a and not b). Since `nand(x, y)` is "not (x and y)", `or_` is `nand(not_(a), not_(b))`.
XOR is 1 when exactly one input is 1: (a or b) and not (a and b). In code: `and_(or_(a, b), nand(a, b))`. The 4-NAND version is: `n = nand(a, b)`, then `nand(nand(a, n), nand(b, n))`.

options.why: AND of 0 and 0 is 0, and NAND flips it to 1. NAND is 0 only when both inputs are 1.
That's AND. NAND is the opposite of AND.
A gate is a fixed function. The truth table says exactly what it outputs for every input.

quiz.q: Why can NAND alone build every other gate?

options.text: You can make NOT from it, plus AND or OR, and those can express any truth table
options.why: NOT plus AND (or NOT plus OR) is enough for any logic function. NAND gives you NOT via nand(a, a), then AND via not_(nand(a, b)).

options.text: Because NAND has the most 1s in its truth table
options.why: OR has three 1s too, and OR alone can't make NOT. What matters is being able to invert.

options.text: It can't: you also need XOR
options.why: XOR is built from NAND, and you'll do it in this exercise.
